headline: Strong returns are clear, but whether they justify the premium price divides the room.
answer:
The room agrees on what the data shows. Al Rajhi Bank earns a return on equity of 23.49% [P2], on a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19 [P1]. Trailing EPS is 4.42 SAR and the last price is 62.1 SAR [P1]. The P/E is above every peer shown, which range from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5]. Debt-to-equity of 1.72 sits at the 22.7th percentile of the sector [P2]. Dividend yield is 2.6% [P1].

Share-price behaviour is weaker. The one-year change is -11.54%, from 70.2 to 62.1 SAR [P7]. The six-month return is -10.68% [P1], and the shares sit below both the 50-day and 200-day averages [P1]. The momentum seat's regime score is 35 out of 100 [P4]. Over five years the shares are up 34.24% [P8].

The room splits on whether the premium is earned. Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan read the return on equity as the mark of a dominant franchise, and the pullback as a correction. Lynch calls the price not a bargain but not outrageous, and sees no margin of safety. Marks and Dalio say the multiples need the return to persist, with little cushion if it slips.

Buffett's early payout figure of 97.4% is not in the pack, because the payout metric is marked missing inputs [P2]. The room set it aside. Buffett now says he cannot judge how much is retained, which keeps him from calling the valuation clearly supported.

The data cannot settle how long a 23.49% return on equity lasts [P1]. It holds no earnings growth history, no forward estimates and no credit-cycle or interest-rate data, as Dalio and Lynch noted. The price and technical datasets are also marked stale [P1].

So the data supports the quality of the earnings and returns. Whether it supports the price paid is not settled by the pack.
gaps: The pack gives no payout ratio or net income, so how much of earnings is retained cannot be checked.
There is no earnings growth history or forward estimate, so the room cannot judge whether the premium P/E is too high, fair or a bargain.
There is no data on credit growth, government spending or the interest-rate path, so the durability of the 23.49% return on equity cannot be gauged [P1].
disagreements: Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan see the premium multiples as earned by a leading franchise, while Marks and Dalio see little margin of safety if returns slip.
Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan read the share-price decline as a correction, while Marks and Dalio read the weak trend and momentum score as a warning.
Buffett cannot confirm that earnings are being retained, while Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan point to the bonus-share issue as evidence of retention.

headline: Earnings and returns look strong, but the data cannot fully confirm the valuation is supported.
answer:
The pack shows a bank with high profitability: return on equity of 23.49% and return on assets of 2.53% [P1]. The trailing price-to-earnings ratio is 14.51x, price-to-book is 3.19x and earnings per share (trailing) is 4.42 SAR [P1]. The council's rule-based quality seat votes bullish because ROE is above its 20% threshold, while the value seat is neutral because the P/E sits below 16 but above 10 [P4].

The room agrees on two points. First, returns on equity are high. Second, the valuation is not cheap relative to the Saudi banks listed in the pack. Peers show P/E ratios between 7.78x and 11.94x, against 14.51x here [P5][P1]. Dividend yield is 2.6% here, while peers range from 3.1% to 6.02% [P1][P5]. The pack gives no sector percentile for P/E, P/B, ROE or yield [P2], so the peer comparison rests on the raw peer list only. It was also taken on 2026-08-07, earlier than the latest quote [P5][P1].

Price behaviour is less supportive. Returns are -10.68% over 6 months and 2.46% over 12 months [P1]. The price is below both the 50-day and 200-day averages, and the momentum seat votes bearish [P1][P4]. The risk seat is neutral at 20.94% one-year volatility [P4].

One caution on the analyst's note: its 97.4 per cent payout ratio is a calculation not found in the pack, and the pack's own payout field is missing [P2]. We therefore do not rely on it. The pack does record a bonus share issue on 2026-04-20 that raised capital from 40000.0 to 60000.0 million SAR [P3], which makes comparing per-share figures across dates uncertain.

Overall: returns support a premium to peers, yet the data does not show that earnings growth justifies the gap, and several inputs are stale.
gaps: The pack shows no earnings growth history or forecasts, so it cannot show whether the P/E is backed by rising profits.
The payout ratio is missing from the pack, so dividend cover cannot be judged from the data.
Peer ROE figures and sector percentiles are absent, so the return premium over peers cannot be measured.
Prices and peer data are stale or dated earlier than the latest quote, so the current valuation may differ.
disagreements: Quality reads bullish on high ROE, while value is only neutral because the P/E is well above the peer range.
Strong profitability points one way, while the weak 6-month return and bearish momentum point the other.
Whether the premium to peers on P/E reflects superior returns or simply a richer price cannot be separated with this data.

headline: Returns are clearly strong, but whether the premium valuation is supported turns on growth the data lacks.
answer:
The data shows a bank with high returns. Return on equity is 23.49% and return on assets is 2.53% [P1]. Trailing EPS is 4.42 SAR, the P/E is 14.51 and the price-to-book is 3.19 at a price of 62.10 SAR [P1]. Debt-to-equity of 1.72 sits in the 22.7th sector percentile [P2], which Buffett, Lynch and Marks read as a sound balance sheet.

The room agrees on three points. The returns mark a high-quality franchise. The P/E is above the peers listed, such as Saudi National Bank (SNB) at 9.48 and Riyad Bank at 7.78 [P5]. The dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is a modest cushion. Marks and Alwaleed add that the premium looks already priced in. Alwaleed notes that the 1-year return of 2.46% and the distance below the 52-week high of -14.92% [P1] do not show a crisis price.

The room splits in three places. Lynch holds that the P/E needs earnings growth the pack does not show. Buffett holds that returns of this level justify a better price, and he withdrew his payout argument once it was shown that the payout figure is listed as missing inputs [P2]. The advisors also read the decline differently. Lynch cites the 1-year fall of 11.54% [P7] and the 6-month fall of 10.68% [P1]. Alwaleed cites the 2.46% 1-year return [P1]. The windows differ, and the price and technical data are flagged stale [P1].

The data cannot say whether growth supports the multiple. It holds no earnings growth rate or forecast, and the payout ratio is unpublished [P2]. The ROE figures quoted for peers do not appear in the peer data [P5]. On the evidence in the pack, the returns support a premium, but the pack does not show how large a premium they support.
gaps: The pack has no historical or forward earnings growth rate, so the P/E cannot be compared with growth.
The payout ratio is listed as missing inputs [P2], so dividend coverage cannot be confirmed from the data.
Peer return-on-equity figures are absent from the peer data [P5], so quality cannot be compared directly with peers.
disagreements: Buffett sees the returns and balance sheet as enough to support the premium, while Lynch says the P/E needs a growth case that cannot be verified.
Marks and Alwaleed call the quality premium fully priced against peers, while Buffett accepts paying more for a stronger business.
Lynch reads the 1-year and 6-month price falls as expectations being trimmed, while Alwaleed reads the weak 1-year return and the gap to the 52-week high as a gentle slide.

headline: The data clearly shows past deterioration in profitability and price; whether it continues is not settled.
answer:
On the question of deterioration, the room agrees on the backward-looking record. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2], and the quality seat votes bearish [P4]. The share price fell 62.55% over five years, from SAR 121.00 to SAR 45.32 [P8], and 26.61% over one year [P7]. Marks adds a maximum drawdown of -86.31% [P1]. The momentum seat is also bearish [P4]. On this evidence the room calls the deterioration clear.

The room also agrees the balance sheet shows no visible strain. Debt-to-equity is 0.26 and the current ratio is 1.80 [P2]. Dalio, Lynch and Al-Rumayyan read this as room to absorb further pain.

The room splits on how to read the rest. Lynch and Alwaleed point to the planned sale of the Americas and Europe units, with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6], but they read it differently. Lynch calls it a restructuring, while Alwaleed sees a retreat. Dalio says the macro drivers needed to place this in a cycle are not in the pack, and Al-Rumayyan says the data is silent on permanence. The dividend is read two ways. The latest payment of SAR 1.1 per share follows SAR 1.5 [P3]. Dalio, Marks and Alwaleed treat it as a sign of stress, while Al-Rumayyan calls it a prudent trim. Alwaleed notes the 5.86% yield keeps the income seat bullish [P1][P4].

Buffett withdrew his payout ratio of 97.4 per cent after the pack showed no earnings per share and no payout figure [P1][P2]. Marks notes a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1] and asks whether the decline is already priced in. The pack gives no way to settle that.

In short, the data clearly shows that profitability and price have deteriorated. It does not show whether that is still worsening, at a cyclical trough, or a lasting step down.
gaps: The pack has no earnings per share, payout figure or cash-flow data, so dividend coverage cannot be measured.
The pack has no macro drivers such as feedstock prices or petrochemical demand, so the position in the cycle cannot be placed.
The pack has no standalone profitability for the businesses that remain after the divestitures, so the future earning power of the core is unknown.
disagreements: Lynch reads the planned divestments as a portfolio overhaul, while Alwaleed reads them as a retreat from markets.
Dalio, Marks and Alwaleed read the lower dividend as stress, while Al-Rumayyan reads it as a prudent trim that preserves capital.
Marks sees the price as already embedding weak expectations, while Dalio and Al-Rumayyan say the data cannot show whether the cycle is turning or the decline is permanent.

headline: Price, returns and profitability readings point to weakness, but earnings data is too thin to call it clearly.
answer:

Price weakness is consistent: the 1-year change is -26.61% [P7], the 5-year change is -62.55% [P8], and the 3-month return is -17.671009772% [P1]. The price is below both the 50-day average of 52.8242 and the 200-day average of 55.7738 [P1]. The momentum seat votes bearish with a regime score of 15.0 out of 100 [P4].

Company events fit the same direction. A disclosure dated 2026-01-07 says SABIC will sell Americas and Europe units and expects a SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6]. The latest dividend per share is SAR 1.1 for H1 2026, down from SAR 1.5 for H2 2025 [P3].

The room splits on how to read the balance sheet and income. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.26061782975782133, at the 50.5 sector percentile, and the current ratio is 1.8006209078026552, at the 63.4 percentile [P2]. The income seat is bullish on a dividend yield of 5.86% [P4]. The risk seat is neutral, with 1-year volatility of 24.1350091449% [P1]. Price-to-book is 1.24 [P1]. A falling payout and a firm yield do not by themselves show whether the business is weakening or only reshaping itself.

The analyst's note cites a payout ratio of 97.4 per cent. The pack gives no earnings per share, because the unit is unconfirmed, and no payout figure [P1][P2]. The room therefore cannot rely on that number.

Overall, the weakness in returns and price is clear. Whether it reflects lasting operating decline or a one-off, such as the non-cash loss tied to the unit sales, cannot be settled from this data. Several price and news datasets are also marked stale, so the picture may lag [P1].
gaps: The pack has no earnings per share, P/E, net margin or payout figure, so dividend cover cannot be tested.

No rated news exists in the last 30 days, so recent sentiment is unknown.
Price and technical data are stale, so the latest market reading is uncertain.
disagreements: The quality and momentum seats read the negative ROE and weak trend as deterioration, while the income seat reads the 5.86% yield as support.
Moderate leverage and a current ratio of 1.8006209078026552 point to a sound balance sheet, while negative returns point to weak earnings.
The negative ROE may reflect the announced non-cash loss rather than ongoing operations, and the data cannot separate the two.

headline: The data clearly shows weaker returns; whether the weakness is cyclical or lasting is not settled.
answer:
The data shows deterioration in returns, and it shows it clearly. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2], and the council's quality seat votes bearish on that ROE figure [P4]. Lynch and Marks both point to the share price: it closed at SAR 45.32, against SAR 121.0 five years ago, a fall of 62.55% [P8]. The dividend per share has stepped down from SAR 1.70 in 2024 to SAR 1.10 in the latest payout [P3]. A January 2026 disclosure said SABIC would sell Americas and Europe units and expected an SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6].

The room also agrees that the balance sheet is workable. Debt-to-equity is 0.26, at the 50.5th sector percentile, and the current ratio is 1.80, at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. Buffett withdrew his payout-ratio argument because the pack publishes no confirmed earnings-per-share figure [P1].

The room splits on what the deterioration means. Lynch reads it as shrinkage and cannot call it a simple cyclical trough. Alwaleed reads it as a cyclical profit crunch with the balance sheet intact, and treats the continued dividend, with a yield of 5.86%, as a sign of confidence [P1]. Marks accepts that the business has deteriorated but asks how much the price already reflects. He cites price-to-book of 1.24 and a maximum drawdown of -86.31% [P1][P2]. Lynch answers that a low price is a market reaction, not proof that bad news is exhausted.

The data cannot settle the cycle question. It holds no earnings figure, no commodity or demand series and no forward estimates. Several freshness flags in the pack are marked stale [P1], so the clarity of the weak returns is greater than the clarity of the reason for them.
gaps: The pack has no confirmed earnings per share or trailing earnings, so payout coverage and the scale of the loss cannot be checked.
The pack has no commodity price or demand series, so it cannot show where SABIC sits in the Materials cycle.
The pack does not show whether the units being sold caused the negative returns, or whether returns are stabilising or still worsening.
disagreements: Lynch reads the negative returns as lasting shrinkage, while Alwaleed reads them as a cyclical profit crunch with an intact balance sheet.
Lynch counts the fall in dividend per share as a cut, while Alwaleed treats the continued payout as a sign of board confidence.
Marks says the price may already reflect the deterioration, while Lynch holds that a low price is only a market reaction to it.

headline: Earnings cover the dividend on reported figures, but cash-flow cover and cycle safety remain unproven.
answer:
On reported earnings, the room agrees the dividend is covered. Trailing earnings per share are SAR 1.84 [P1]. The last four quarterly dividends total SAR 1.35 per share, three at SAR 0.34 and one at SAR 0.33 [P3]. Lynch, Marks and Al-Rumayyan put the payout at roughly 73 to 74 per cent. Buffett opened with 97.4 per cent but withdrew it after the challenges, since the pack holds no dividend that produces that figure. The pack itself shows no payout figure, because the metric is marked missing inputs [P2].

The room also agrees on the balance sheet. Debt to equity is 0.20 and the current ratio is near 2.0 [P2]. Return on equity is 26.75% [P1]. Marks and Al-Rumayyan add that the company completed a $4 billion bond issuance in early 2026 [P6]. Everyone treats this as the buffer that buys time in a weaker year.

The room splits on how much that proves. Lynch and Alwaleed read the dividend as covered and safe. Buffett calls a payout of about 73 per cent a thin margin for a cyclical business. Marks and Al-Rumayyan accept earnings cover but say cash-flow cover cannot be seen, because the free cash flow yield is marked na_sector [P2]. Dalio says trailing cover is a rear-view measure and that safety through a cycle depends on drivers the pack does not contain.

The dividend history is read two ways. Marks points to the fall from SAR 0.48 per share in 2024 to SAR 0.33 in 2025 as evidence that cuts happen [P3]. Alwaleed reads the recent SAR 0.34 as board confidence [P3]. Al-Rumayyan separates the base dividend from the performance-linked part, for which the pack gives no coverage data.

In short, the data shows earnings cover and a strong balance sheet. It does not settle whether the dividend is safe through a full cycle.
gaps: The pack shows no free cash flow, so it cannot be seen whether operating cash funds the dividend.
The pack has no multi-year earnings history, so it is unclear how the dividend held through past downturns.
The pack has no oil-price, production or fiscal data, so earnings cannot be stress-tested through a cycle.
disagreements: Lynch and Alwaleed call the dividend covered and safe, while Marks, Dalio and Al-Rumayyan say safety is unproven without cash-flow data.
Buffett regards a payout of about 73 per cent as a thin margin for a cyclical business, whereas Alwaleed sees it as a sign of strength.
Marks reads the earlier fall in the quarterly dividend as proof that cuts are possible, while Alwaleed reads the recent SAR 0.34 as board confidence [P3].

headline: Dividend appears covered on the published figures, but payout and cash-flow evidence is incomplete in this data.
answer:
The question is whether earnings cover the dividend and how safe it looks. The data here answers only part of it.

What the data shows: trailing earnings per share is SAR 1.84 [P1]. The last three quarterly dividends were SAR 0.34 per share each [P3], and the dividend yield is 5.01% [P1]. The pack does not publish a payout ratio; that field is missing [P2]. The analyst's figure of 97.4 per cent is not in the pack and is not a published value. The Chair cannot verify it, so the room does not rely on it. The data also does not show whether the quarterly dividends sum to an annual figure that can be set against earnings per share.

Balance sheet and returns: debt to equity is 0.20 and the current ratio is 2.00, with a health score of 61.2 [P2]. Return on equity is 26.75% and return on assets is 15.86% [P1]. The P/E is 14.47 [P1].

History: the per-share dividend was SAR 0.48 in each 2024 quarter, with performance-linked amounts of SAR 40390 million in the Q3 2024 payout, and SAR 0.33 through 2025 before rising to SAR 0.34 in 2026 [P3]. The payout has therefore been reset once in the period shown, and the data does not say why.

The rule-based seats give the income seat a bullish vote on yield, the risk seat a neutral vote with one-year volatility of 15.50% [P4], and the news seat abstains for lack of rated news [P4].

Where the room agrees: the figures that are published point to profitable operations and modest leverage. Where it cannot settle: the thin or missing payout, free cash flow and coverage fields mean the room cannot confirm the dividend is covered by earnings or by cash. Price and some other data are also stale [P1], so the view is a snapshot, not a current reading.
gaps: The pack gives no published payout ratio, so coverage by earnings cannot be confirmed from it.
Free cash flow yield and interest coverage are not available, so cash cover of the dividend is unknown.
The data does not show why the per-share dividend fell after 2024 or whether the performance-linked element will return.
Price, news and disclosure data are stale, so recent developments may not be reflected.
disagreements: Yield and returns on equity read as supportive, while the missing payout and free cash flow fields leave coverage unconfirmed.
The analyst's very high payout reading suggests thin cover, whereas the published balance sheet ratios suggest ample capacity, and the pack cannot reconcile the two.

headline: Trailing earnings cover the base dividend, but how safe it is through a downturn stays unresolved.
answer:
The pack shows trailing earnings per share of SAR 1.84 [P1] and a base quarterly dividend of SAR 0.34 per share for the last three quarters [P3]. The pack's own payout field is missing [P2], so every coverage ratio in the room is advisor arithmetic. Lynch and Alwaleed annualised the base dividend to SAR 1.36 against that EPS, a payout of about 74 per cent [P1][P3]. Marks summed the last four paid quarters to SAR 1.34, a payout of roughly 73 per cent [P3]. Buffett opened with 97.4 per cent, then withdrew it because it could not be built from the dividends in the pack.

The room agrees on three points. The base dividend is covered by trailing earnings. Leverage is low, with debt-to-equity of 0.20 and a current ratio near 2.0 [P2]. The pack gives no forward earnings.

The room splits on how thin the margin is. Lynch calls the coverage comfortable. Alwaleed says it is not wide but leaves room. Buffett and Marks hold that for a cyclical energy company a payout near 74 per cent leaves too little room for a weaker year. Marks pointed to the maximum drawdown of -40.14% [P1] as a sign the market has priced in severe downside before, and to a P/E of 14.47 [P1] that does not appear to discount a risk to the dividend. Lynch and Alwaleed read the balance sheet as enough to carry the payout through a cycle, while Marks and Buffett say a strong balance sheet does not guarantee a dividend.

The data cannot say how earnings or cash flow behaved in earlier downturns, what forward earnings look like, or whether free cash flow and interest coverage support the payout, since those fields are unavailable [P2]. The next dividend announcement was named by Marks as a test of the trend.
gaps: The pack does not show forward earnings, so it cannot test whether coverage holds if earnings fall.
The pack does not show earnings, payout or cash flow during the past drawdown or any earlier downturn.
Free cash flow yield, interest coverage and the payout ratio are unavailable, so coverage from cash flow cannot be confirmed [P2].
disagreements: Buffett and Marks see a payout near 74 per cent as thin for a cyclical business, while Lynch sees it as comfortable and Alwaleed sees it as covered with room.

Lynch and Alwaleed treat low leverage and a current ratio near 2.0 as enough protection, whereas Marks says the balance sheet only decides how a shortfall is funded and the drawdown of -40.14% is a warning [P1].
The advisors use different dividend sums (SAR 1.36 versus SAR 1.34) and the pack's payout field is missing, so no single coverage ratio is agreed.
